title: The Tinsmith Who Invented Korea's Movable Type
event_summary: During the Mongol invasions of the Goryeo Kingdom, government craftsmen — metalworkers and tinsmiths working under minister Choe Yun-ui — cast the world's first known metal movable type to reprint the massive Buddhist scripture collection 'Sangjeong Gogeum Yemun.' Nearly two centuries before Gutenberg's press, Korean artisans solved the engineering problem of casting uniform, reusable metal characters, printing texts that were distributed across Buddhist monasteries. The original printed works were destroyed during subsequent Mongol raids, but records in the 'Dongguk Isanggukjip' confirm their existence.
why_forgotten: The printed texts themselves were lost to Mongol destruction, leaving only secondary references, which made Western historians skeptical or dismissive for centuries. European historiography long centered Gutenberg as the singular inventor of movable type, and Cold War-era division of Korea further marginalized Korean claims to international scholarly attention. Japan's colonial occupation of Korea (1910-1945) also systematically suppressed Korean cultural achievements.
why_it_matters: This event proves that the information revolution — the ability to mass-produce identical texts cheaply — was not a uniquely European innovation but emerged independently in East Asia under conditions of existential crisis. Korea's Jikji, printed with metal type in 1377 and now held at the Bibliothèque nationale de France, is the oldest surviving metal-type printed book, recognized by UNESCO. Understanding this shifts the entire narrative of how knowledge dissemination shaped civilization, undermining Eurocentric models of technological progress that still dominate education worldwide.
